intro: A soccer ball rolls across the grass and stops. A magnet grabs a paper clip from across a gap. A marble dropped from a shelf knocks over a whole line of dominoes. Every one of these is a puzzle about forces and energy. Forces are the pushes and pulls that start, stop and turn things. Energy is what makes anything happen at all.

In this unit you will draw a force as an arrow. The arrow shows a strength and a direction. You will find out why balanced forces leave motion alone. You will see why unbalanced forces change it. You will meet gravity, friction, magnets and static electricity. Then you will follow energy as it moves. It travels in a collision, as sound, as light, as heat, and through wires.

By the end, you will look at a moving thing and predict what it does next. You will also design something of your own. It might be a magnetic latch or a solar oven. Then you will test it fairly. The evidence comes from simple things. A string and a washer. A ramp and a ball. A battery and a bulb.
bigQuestion: How do forces change motion, and how does energy move from one place to another?

timeline.t: William Gilbert publishes De Magnete and argues that Earth itself is a giant magnet
Galileo publishes his ramp experiments showing how falling objects speed up in a pattern
Christiaan Huygens builds the first pendulum clock
Isaac Newton publishes the Principia with his three laws of motion
Benjamin Franklin's kite experiment shows that lightning is electricity
Count Rumford watches cannons being bored and argues that heat is motion
Alessandro Volta describes the first battery, a pile of metal disks
Michael Faraday shows that a moving magnet can make electricity flow in a wire
James Joule measures how much heat a set amount of motion can make
Thomas Edison demonstrates a long-lasting electric light bulb
Bell Labs makes the first practical solar cell that turns sunlight into electricity

words.d: a push or a pull on an object
forces that cancel out, so the object's motion does not change
forces that do not cancel, so the object speeds up, slows down or turns
a pull between objects with mass; Earth's gravity pulls things toward its center
a force that slows things that rub together
an object that pulls on iron and steel and can push or pull other magnets
extra electric charge that builds up on an object, often from rubbing
the ability to make something happen, such as moving, warming or lighting an object
when two objects hit each other and energy passes between them
energy an object holds and can release later, such as a raised marble or a battery
a complete loop that electricity can flow around
a material that slows the movement of heat, such as foam, wool or trapped air

test.q: Two teams pull a rope with equal strength in opposite directions. The rope does not move. Why?
test.why: Equal pulls in opposite directions cancel out, so the rope's motion does not change.

test.q: Which force pulls a dropped pencil to the floor?
test.why: Gravity pulls every object toward the center of Earth.

test.q: A sled slides across snow and slows down. Which force is slowing it?
test.why: Friction between the sled and the snow pushes against the motion.

test.q: A pendulum with a short string is swapped for one with a long string. What changes?
choices: The long one takes more time per swing
test.why: A longer string makes each swing take longer. The washer's weight does not matter.

test.q: What did Galileo find about the speed of a ball rolling down a ramp?
choices: It keeps increasing in a regular pattern
test.why: The distances grew by odd numbers, 1, 3, 5, 7, showing a steady speeding up.

test.q: Which pair of magnet poles will pull together?
test.why: Opposite poles attract. Like poles repel.

test.q: A balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a wall. What force holds it?
test.why: Rubbing built up charge on the balloon, and that charge pulls on the wall.

test.q: Which object carries the most motion energy?
test.why: Motion energy grows with both mass and speed. The fast bowling ball has the most of both.

test.q: A cue ball hits another ball and stops while the other rolls away. What happened to the energy?
choices: It moved to the second ball
It stayed in the cue ball
test.why: In a collision, energy is transferred from one object to the other.

test.q: Which of these is storing energy for later?
test.why: A battery holds energy in its chemicals until a circuit lets it out.

test.q: How does light from the Sun differ from sound from a bell?
choices: Light can travel through empty space
test.why: Sound needs air, water or a solid to travel through. Light crosses empty space.

test.q: A hot spoon is dropped into cold water. What happens?
choices: Heat moves from the water to the spoon
Heat moves from the spoon to the water until both match
test.why: Heat always moves from the warmer object to the cooler one until they reach the same temperature.

test.q: A bulb in a circuit goes dark when a wire is unhooked. Why?
choices: The loop is broken, so the flow stops
The battery is now too strong
test.why: Electricity needs a complete loop. Unhooking a wire opens a gap.

test.q: A motor in a circuit changes electricity into what?
test.why: A motor uses electricity and magnets to spin, so it makes motion.

test.q: A class wants to know if black paper makes a solar oven hotter. What is the best test?
choices: Change the paper and the box size at once
Test once and trust the result
Build two different ovens with no plan
Change only the paper color and keep everything else the same
test.why: A fair test changes only one thing, so the result has one clear cause.

write.prompt: Make a claim: does the height a marble starts from change how much energy it gives to what it hits? Use evidence from the marble run story, the ramp lessons, and your own tests to support your claim.
tips: Claim: state in one sentence what starting height does to the marble's energy.
Evidence: use the marble run story, Galileo's ramp pattern, and any data table from your own tests.
Reasoning: explain how stored energy from height becomes motion energy, then passes on in a collision.
The other side: what could make a higher start give less energy to the target, such as friction or the marble flying off the track?

title: Forces, Motion and Energy

chapters.title: Forces and Motion
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we predict what a push or a pull will do to an object?

story.title: The Rope That Would Not Move
story.kicker: Twenty kids pulled as hard as they could, and the flag in the middle stayed right where it was.
paragraphs: It was field day at a school on Chicago's South Side. Two teams of ten grabbed a thick rope. A red flag was tied to the middle. A chalk line on the grass marked the center. The teacher yelled, "Pull!" Everyone leaned back. Faces turned red. Shoes dug into the dirt. And the flag did not move. Not one inch.

This seemed strange. Twenty kids were pulling with all their strength. The rope was stretched tight. Yet nothing changed. If you looked only at the flag, you might think nobody was pulling at all. But the kids' shaking arms told a different story. Something big was happening. It just was not motion.

Then one girl on the left team slipped. Her foot skidded on a patch of mud. For one second her pull was gone. Right away the flag jumped toward the right team. The whole left team stumbled forward. The right team fell in a heap, laughing. The chalk line was far behind the flag now.

That one slip tells you almost everything about forces. Two pulls that match each other cancel out. The rope goes nowhere. But make one pull a little stronger, and motion starts at once. Scientists have a name for each case. This chapter is about those names and the patterns behind them.
story.think: The flag did not move at first. Does that mean no force was acting on it? What is your evidence?

lessons.title: What a Force Is
lessons.mainIdea: A force is a push or a pull, and every force has a strength and a direction.
reading: Kick a soccer ball and it rolls away. Pull a wagon and it follows you. Both of these are examples of a *force*. A force is simply a push or a pull. You cannot see a force itself. You can only see what it does to an object. When you watch something start, stop, speed up, or turn, a force is at work.

Every force has two parts. The first is *strength*. A gentle tap on a ball is a weak force. A hard kick is a strong force. The second part is *direction*. A push to the left and a push to the right are different forces. Scientists draw a force as an arrow. A longer arrow means a stronger push. The arrow points the way the push goes.

Try this with a door. Push it near the handle and it swings easily. Push the same door right next to the hinges and it will barely budge. Same strength, different place, different result. Where and which way you push matters as much as how hard. When we describe a force, we always name both its strength and its direction.

words.d: a push or a pull on an object
how hard a force pushes or pulls
the way a force pushes or pulls, such as left, right, up or down

look.title: Arrows on a Shopping Cart
look.text: Picture a shopping cart in a parking lot. A child pushes it gently from behind. At the same time, the wind pushes it from the side. Draw the cart from above. Draw one arrow for the child's push and one for the wind. Make the child's arrow longer, because that push is stronger.
look.prompt: Which way do you think the cart will roll? Why not straight ahead?

check.q: What is a force?
choices: A kind of energy stored in food
check.why: A force is a push or a pull. You see it by what it does to an object.

check.q: Two students push a box with the same strength but in different directions. What is different about their forces?
choices: Nothing; the forces are the same
check.why: Every force has a strength and a direction. Here the strengths match, so the direction is what differs.

check.q: Why does a door open easily near the handle but not near the hinges?
choices: The push near the handle is stronger
The push near the hinges is in the wrong place to turn the door
check.why: The strength was the same. Where and which way you push changes what the force does.

lessons.title: Balanced Forces
lessons.mainIdea: When forces on an object are balanced, they cancel out and the object's motion does not change.
reading: Think back to the tug-of-war. Both teams pulled hard, but the flag stayed still. The two pulls were equal in strength and opposite in direction. We call forces like this *balanced*. Balanced forces *cancel* each other out. It is as if no force were acting at all. The flag did not move because there was no leftover pull in any direction.

Balanced forces are everywhere. A book sits on a table. Gravity pulls the book down. The table pushes the book up with exactly the same strength. The book stays put. You sit in a chair right now. The chair pushes up as hard as your weight pushes down. If it did not, you would sink through it.

Here is a surprise. Balanced forces do not only keep things still. They also keep moving things moving at a steady speed. A hockey puck sliding on very smooth ice keeps going in a straight line. No force is winning. The puck's motion does not change. Balanced forces mean no change, whether the object is resting or moving.

words.d: forces that are equal in strength and opposite in direction
to undo each other so the total effect is zero

look.title: Newton's First Law
look.text: Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a right line, unless it is compelled to change that state by forces impressed thereon.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia, 1687, in Andrew Motte's English translation of 1729
look.prompt: Put Newton's sentence in your own words. What does 'perseveres in its state of rest' mean for the flag in the tug-of-war?

check.q: Which situation shows balanced forces?
choices: A book resting on a table
A ball rolling faster down a hill
A bike slowing to a stop
check.why: Gravity pulls the book down and the table pushes it up just as hard. Its motion does not change.

check.q: A puck slides across smooth ice at a steady speed in a straight line. What is true about the forces on it?
choices: A strong force keeps pushing it forward
The forces are balanced, so its motion does not change
No forces at all touch the puck
check.why: Gravity and the ice's push cancel. With balanced forces, steady motion stays steady.

check.q: Why does a table hold a book up instead of letting it fall?
choices: Gravity stops working on the table
The table pushes up on the book as hard as gravity pulls down
The book is too light for gravity
check.why: The table's upward push balances gravity's downward pull, so the book stays still.

lessons.title: Unbalanced Forces Change Motion
lessons.mainIdea: An unbalanced force makes an object speed up, slow down, or change direction.
reading: When the girl in the tug-of-war slipped, the pulls stopped matching. The right team's pull was now stronger. The forces were *unbalanced*. The rope moved toward the stronger pull right away. Any time forces do not cancel, motion changes. This is the rule that lets you predict what happens next.

An unbalanced force can change motion in three ways. It can make an object start or speed up. Think of a kick on a still ball. It can make an object slow down or stop. Think of a catcher's mitt on a pitch. Or it can change direction, like a bat sending a pitch into the air. In each case, look for the force that is not being canceled.

The size of the change depends on two things. A stronger force makes a bigger change. A heavier object changes less for the same force. Push a shopping cart that is empty and it zips away. Push a full one with the same strength and it barely moves. Scientists call the amount of stuff in an object its *mass*. More mass means harder to change.

words.d: forces that do not cancel, so one direction wins
the amount of matter in an object; more mass makes it harder to speed up or slow down

look.title: The Slip
look.text: Imagine watching the tug-of-war in slow motion. Before the slip, the arrows on each side are the same length and point opposite ways. Then the girl's foot skids. Her arrow disappears. The left team's total arrow is now shorter than the right team's. Draw the two arrows before the slip and after.
look.prompt: After the slip, which way does the flag move? What would happen if the left team had twice as many students?

check.q: A rolling ball on the floor slows down and stops. What must be true?
choices: An unbalanced force acted against its motion
check.why: Motion changed, so the forces were unbalanced. Friction pushed against the rolling.

check.q: You push an empty cart and then a full cart with the same strength. What happens?
choices: The empty cart speeds up more because it has less mass
Both carts speed up the same amount
The full cart speeds up more because it is heavier
check.why: The same force changes the motion of a low-mass object more than a high-mass one.

check.q: Which is an example of a force changing an object's direction?
choices: A car sitting at a red light
A bat hitting a pitched baseball
A book resting on a desk
A puck sliding at a steady speed
check.why: The bat's push sends the ball a new way. The other examples show no change in motion.

lessons.title: Gravity Pulls Everything Down
lessons.mainIdea: Gravity is a pull toward the center of Earth that acts on every object, all the time.
reading: Drop a pencil and it falls to the floor. It never falls up or sideways. The force that pulls it is *gravity*. Gravity is a pull between objects that have mass. Earth has an enormous mass. So Earth pulls hard on everything near it. The pull always points toward Earth's center. That is what we mean by "down."

You feel gravity as *weight*. Your weight is the strength of Earth's pull on you. A scale measures that pull. Gravity acts even when you are not falling. Stand still, and gravity pulls you down while the floor pushes you up. Jump, and for a moment the floor stops pushing. Gravity wins, and you come back down.

Gravity does not need to touch you. It pulls across empty space. That is how Earth keeps the Moon circling around it. It is also why a ball thrown up always comes back. As the ball rises, gravity slows it. At the top it stops for an instant. Then gravity pulls it faster and faster toward the ground.

words.d: a pull between objects that have mass; Earth's gravity pulls things toward its center
the strength of gravity's pull on an object

look.title: How Hard Different Worlds Pull
look.prompt: A student weighs 60 pounds on Earth. Roughly what would a scale read on the Moon? On Jupiter?

check.q: Which way does gravity pull an object near Earth?
check.why: Gravity always pulls toward Earth's center. That direction is what we call down.

check.q: What does a bathroom scale measure?
choices: The strength of Earth's pull on you
check.why: Weight is the strength of gravity's pull on you, and that is what the scale reads.

check.q: A ball is thrown straight up. What does gravity do while the ball rises?
choices: Turns off until the ball stops
check.why: Gravity keeps pulling down the whole time, so the rising ball slows until it stops and falls.

lessons.title: Friction Slows Things Down
lessons.mainIdea: Friction is a force between surfaces that rub, and it always pushes against the motion.
reading: Slide a book across a table. It stops after a short distance. Slide it across ice and it goes much farther. The force that stopped the book is *friction*. Friction happens when two surfaces rub against each other. Even smooth-looking surfaces have tiny bumps. The bumps catch on each other and resist the motion.

Friction always pushes against the direction of motion. That makes it a great brake. Bike brakes squeeze rubber pads against the wheel. Car tires grip the road. Sandpaper grips wood. In Chicago winters, crews spread salt and sand on icy sidewalks. The grit adds friction so shoes and tires can hold on.

Sometimes we want less friction. Oil on a bike chain lets it spin freely. Wax on a sled lets it fly down the hill. A hockey rink is kept smooth so pucks glide. *Rough* surfaces make more friction. *Smooth* surfaces make less. Engineers add friction where things must grip and remove it where things must slide.

words.d: a force that slows things that rub together
bumpy or uneven; rough surfaces make more friction
flat and even; smooth surfaces make less friction

look.title: Same Push, Four Floors
look.text: A student pushes a wooden block with the same strength on four surfaces: a carpet, a wood floor, a tile floor, and a sheet of ice. On carpet the block goes 20 centimeters. On wood it goes 60. On tile it goes 90. On ice it slides across the whole room.
look.prompt: Rank the four surfaces from most friction to least. What do you think would happen with a rubber block instead of wood?

check.q: Why does a sliding book stop on a table?
choices: Friction between the book and table pushes against its motion
The book runs out of energy inside
The table pulls it toward the middle
check.why: Friction acts against the motion. It slows the book until it stops.

check.q: Why do road crews spread sand on icy sidewalks?
choices: To melt the ice with heat
To add friction so shoes can grip
check.why: Grit makes the surface rougher, and rougher surfaces have more friction.

check.q: Where would a sled slide the farthest with the same push?
check.why: Ice is the smoothest surface, so it has the least friction to slow the sled.

lessons.title: The Swing of a Pendulum
lessons.mainIdea: A pendulum swings in a repeating pattern, and that pattern lets you predict its next swing.
reading: Tie a washer to a string and let it hang. Pull it to the side and let go. It swings back and forth, back and forth. This is a *pendulum*. Gravity pulls the washer down toward the middle. It overshoots, rises on the other side, and gravity pulls it back. The swings get smaller as air friction steals a bit of motion each time.

Time the swings and you will find a *pattern*. Each full swing takes almost the same time as the one before. A short string swings quickly. A long string swings slowly. Strangely, a heavy washer and a light washer on the same string keep the same time. The length is what matters, not the weight.

Once you know the pattern, you can *predict*. If ten swings took 20 seconds, the next ten will take about 20 seconds too. Long ago, people used this pattern to build clocks. A swinging pendulum ticked off the seconds. Any time motion repeats, watch for the pattern. The pattern is what makes the future easy to guess.

words.d: a weight hanging from a string or rod that swings back and forth
something that repeats in a way you can count on
to say what will happen before it happens, using a pattern or evidence

look.title: Longer String, Slower Swing
look.prompt: What happens to the swing time when the string gets four times longer? Predict the time for a 9 m string.

check.q: Which change makes a pendulum swing more slowly?
check.why: The length of the string sets the swing time. Longer strings swing more slowly.

check.q: Ten swings of a pendulum took 15 seconds. About how long will the next ten swings take?
check.why: Each swing takes about the same time, so the pattern repeats: about 15 seconds.

check.q: What force pulls the pendulum back toward the middle on every swing?
check.why: Gravity pulls the washer down toward the lowest point every time it rises.

lessons.title: A Ball on a Ramp
lessons.mainIdea: A ball speeds up as it rolls down a ramp in a steady pattern that Galileo measured and you can measure too.
reading: Roll a ball down a *ramp*. It starts slow and gets faster and faster. Gravity pulls it down the slope the whole way. The pull is steady, so the speed keeps growing. About 400 years ago, an Italian scientist named Galileo studied this. He wanted to know exactly how falling objects speed up. Free fall was too fast to time. So he slowed it down with a ramp.

Galileo rolled bronze balls down a long, smooth groove. He timed each roll. He found a clear *pattern*. In the second stretch of time, the ball went three times as far as in the first. In the third, five times as far. The distance grew by odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7. This pattern held no matter how steep the ramp was.

You can test this yourself. Mark a ramp every 10 centimeters. Let the ball go and count out loud at a steady beat. Notice where the ball is on each count. Then make the ramp steeper and try again. A steeper ramp means a bigger pull down the slope. The ball speeds up faster. But the odd-number pattern shows up again. Patterns like this let scientists *predict* motion before it happens.

words.d: a sloped surface that an object can roll or slide along
something that repeats in a way you can count on
to say what will happen before it happens, using a pattern or evidence

look.title: Galileo's Groove
look.text: Galileo describes a wooden beam about 12 cubits long with a smooth, straight groove cut into it and lined with parchment. He rolled a hard, smooth bronze ball down the groove and timed each roll by weighing the water that dripped from a bucket while the ball moved. He repeated each roll many times, and found that the distances always grew with the square of the time.
look.cite: Galileo Galilei, Two New Sciences, 1638 (paraphrased from the 1914 English translation)
look.prompt: Why did Galileo repeat each roll many times instead of trusting one measurement?

check.q: Why did Galileo use a ramp instead of dropping balls straight down?
choices: He did not own a tall tower
A ramp slows the motion enough to time it
check.why: Free fall was too fast for his clocks. A gentle slope made the same kind of motion slow enough to measure.

check.q: A ball rolls down a ramp. What happens to its speed as it goes?
check.why: Gravity keeps pulling the ball down the slope, so it keeps speeding up.

check.q: If a ball travels 1 unit in the first count and 3 units in the second, how far will it travel in the third count if the pattern holds?
check.why: Galileo's pattern grows by odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7. The third stretch is 5 units.

lessons.title: Magnets Push and Pull
lessons.mainIdea: A magnet can push or pull certain objects without touching them, and its two poles behave differently.
reading: Hold a magnet near a paper clip. The clip jumps across the gap and sticks. Nothing touched the clip until it moved. The pull came from the *magnet* itself. Magnets attract some metals, mostly iron and steel. They ignore copper, aluminum, wood, and plastic. Test this around you. A steel refrigerator door will hold a magnet, but an aluminum soda can will not.

Every magnet has two ends called *poles*, north and south. Bring two north poles together and they push apart. You can feel the push in your fingers. Turn one magnet around and the north and south poles snap together. Opposite poles *attract*. Like poles *repel*. The push and pull get stronger as the magnets get closer.

Earth itself acts like a giant magnet. That is why a compass needle turns to point north. Sailors used compasses for hundreds of years before anyone knew why they worked. In the year 1600, an English doctor named William Gilbert tested lodestones, which are natural magnets. He argued that the whole Earth was one great magnet. His evidence was the compass.

words.d: an object that pulls on iron and steel and can push or pull other magnets
the two ends of a magnet, called north and south
to pull toward
to push away

look.title: Gilbert's Little Earth
look.text: In his 1600 book on magnets, William Gilbert described shaping a lodestone into a ball he called a terrella, or 'little Earth.' When he moved a small compass needle around the ball, the needle turned the way compass needles do on the real Earth. From this he argued that Earth itself is a great magnet.
look.prompt: What did Gilbert observe, and what idea did he build from that observation?

check.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
check.why: Magnets attract iron and steel. Copper, plastic, and wood are not attracted.

check.q: You bring the north pole of one magnet near the north pole of another. What happens?
check.why: Like poles repel. Two north poles push away from each other.

check.q: Why does a compass needle point north?
choices: Earth acts like a giant magnet
The needle is heavier on one end
check.why: The needle is a small magnet, and Earth's magnetism turns it toward the north.

lessons.title: Static Electricity
lessons.mainIdea: Rubbing some materials together builds up static electricity, which can push or pull objects without touching them.
reading: Rub a balloon on your hair. Hold it near a wall and it sticks. Hold it near tiny bits of paper and they leap up. Your hair may even stand on end. This is *static electricity*. Rubbing moves tiny bits of electric *charge* from one object to the other. The balloon ends up with extra charge. The extra charge pulls on the paper from a distance.

There are two kinds of charge, called positive and negative. Like charges push apart. Opposite charges pull together. That sounds a lot like magnets. But charge and magnetism are not the same thing. A charged balloon does not pick up a paper clip. A magnet does not attract paper bits. Each one has its own kind of force.

In a dry Chicago winter, static shows up everywhere. Pull off a wool hat and your hair crackles. Touch a doorknob and you feel a tiny zap. The zap is a little spark. Charge that built up on you jumps to the metal. Lightning is the same thing on a giant scale. Charge builds in a storm cloud and then jumps in one huge spark.

words.d: extra electric charge that builds up on an object, often from rubbing
a property of tiny particles that makes them push or pull on each other; it comes in positive and negative

look.title: Sparks From a Key
look.text: In a 1752 letter, Benjamin Franklin described flying a kite with a pointed wire during a thunderstorm. A metal key hung from the kite string. Once the string grew wet, he wrote, sparks could be drawn from the key with a knuckle, just like the sparks from a rubbed glass tube. This was his evidence that lightning was electric.
look.cite: Benjamin Franklin, letter to Peter Collinson, 1752 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What did Franklin compare the spark from the key to? Why did that comparison matter?

check.q: What happens when you rub a balloon on your hair?
choices: Charge moves between the hair and the balloon
check.why: Rubbing moves charge from one object to the other. That extra charge is static electricity.

check.q: Two objects both carry negative charge. What will they do?
check.why: Like charges repel, so two negative objects push away from each other.

check.q: What is the tiny zap you feel when touching a doorknob?
choices: A small spark of charge jumping to the metal
check.why: Charge that built up on you jumps to the metal knob as a tiny spark.

lessons.title: Solving a Problem With Magnets
lessons.mainIdea: Engineers use pushes and pulls, like the pull of a magnet, to design solutions to everyday problems.
reading: A cabinet door in a classroom keeps swinging open. Books fall out. The class decides to fix it. They need something that holds the door shut but lets it open with a small pull. A magnet is perfect. A small magnet on the frame and a steel plate on the door make a *latch*. The magnet's pull holds the door. A tug stronger than that pull opens it.

This is *engineering*: using science to solve a problem. First the class defines the problem clearly. The door must stay shut on its own but open easily. Then they test ideas. One magnet is too weak; the door drifts open. Three magnets are too strong; small hands cannot open it. Two magnets are just right. Testing tells them which design works.

Magnets solve many problems this way. Refrigerator doors seal with a magnetic strip. Some phone chargers snap on with magnets. Cranes in scrap yards lift whole cars with huge electromagnets. Some trains float above their tracks on magnetic pushes. Every one of these designs started with a problem and a test.

words.d: a device that holds a door or lid closed
using science and testing to design a solution to a problem

look.title: Design a Better Latch
look.text: Your class has three magnets of different strengths, a steel plate, tape, and a cabinet door that keeps swinging open. A first-grade class will use the cabinet. Their hands are small and not very strong. You need the door to stay closed when the room is bumped, but open with one finger.
look.prompt: Which magnet would you try first, and how would you test whether it is too strong or too weak?

check.q: What holds a magnetic latch closed?
choices: The pull between the magnet and the steel plate
Friction between the door and frame
check.why: The magnet attracts the steel plate. That pull keeps the door shut until a stronger tug opens it.

check.q: The class found one magnet was too weak and three were too strong. What did they learn from testing?
choices: Magnets do not work on doors
Two magnets would likely be the right strength
The door needs a lock instead
check.why: Testing showed the right strength was between one and three magnets.

check.q: What is the first step in solving an engineering problem?
choices: Define clearly what the solution must do
check.why: A clear problem tells you what to test for. Then you can tell if a design works.

review.q: In the tug-of-war story, why did the flag stay still at first?
choices: The two teams' pulls were balanced
review.why: Equal pulls in opposite directions cancel out, so the flag's motion did not change.

review.q: What two things describe every force?
review.why: A force is drawn as an arrow: its length is the strength and it points in the direction.

review.q: A soccer ball rolls across grass and slows to a stop. Which force slows it?
review.why: Friction between the ball and the grass pushes against the motion.

review.q: Which of these shows an unbalanced force at work?
choices: A lamp sitting on a desk
A puck gliding at a steady speed
A sled speeding up down a hill
review.why: Speeding up is a change in motion, and only unbalanced forces change motion.

review.q: A pendulum with a 1 m string takes 2 seconds per swing. Which pendulum would take longer?
review.why: Longer strings swing more slowly. The weight of the washer does not change the time.

choices: A north pole and a south pole
A magnet and a paper clip
A magnet and a steel door
review.why: Like poles repel. Opposite poles and magnets near steel attract.

review.q: What did Galileo's ramp experiments show about a rolling ball?
choices: It moves at a constant speed
It slows down as it rolls
It speeds up in a regular pattern
review.why: The distances grew by odd numbers, 1, 3, 5, 7, showing a steady speeding up.

review.q: A charged balloon sticks to a wall. What makes it stick?
choices: Static electricity pulling from a distance
review.why: The extra charge on the balloon pulls on the wall without touching it.

chapters.title: Energy on the Move
chapters.bigQuestion: Where does energy come from, and how does it move from one place to another?

story.title: The Marble Run That Took a Whole Saturday
story.kicker: A tall tower of cardboard tubes, one marble, and a question nobody in the house could answer.
paragraphs: Rain kept two cousins inside one Saturday in a Chicago apartment. They found a bag of marbles and a pile of paper towel tubes. By noon the kitchen wall was covered in tubes taped in a zigzag. A marble dropped in at the top rattled all the way down. It shot out the bottom and hit a row of dominoes. The dominoes fell, one by one, and knocked a small bell off a shelf. Ding.

The cousins wanted the marble to go faster. They made the top of the run taller. The marble came out with more speed. It knocked the dominoes down harder. But then it flew right off the table, and the bell did not ring at all. They added a curved tube at the bottom to catch it. Now the marble slowed and rolled to the dominoes gently.

Then the little cousin asked a good question. The marble just sat there at the top, still. Where did its speed come from? The older cousin said gravity pulled it down. But a marble lying on the floor is pulled by gravity too, and it does not move. There had to be something else. Something the marble had when it was up high that it did not have on the floor.

The something has a name: energy. The higher the marble started, the more energy it had to give. It gave that energy to the dominoes in a collision. The dominoes gave it to the bell. The bell gave it to the air as sound, and the sound reached their ears. By dinner the marble run was a lesson. Energy had moved from the top of the tower to their ears, one step at a time.
story.think: Trace the energy from the top of the marble tower all the way to the bell's ring. Where do you think some of it got lost along the way?

lessons.title: Faster Means More Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Energy is the ability to make things happen, and a faster-moving object carries more energy.
reading: A slow marble nudges a domino. A fast marble knocks it flying. The fast marble carries more *energy*. Energy is what lets an object make something happen. It can move a thing, warm a thing, light a thing, or break a thing. You cannot see energy itself, but you can see its effects. The bigger the effect, the more energy was used.

The energy of a moving object is called *motion energy*. It depends on two things. One is how fast the object moves. The other is how much mass it has. Double the speed and the energy grows a lot, more than double. A bike at 20 miles per hour has four times the motion energy it had at 10. That is why a fall at high speed hurts so much more.

Mass matters too. A bowling ball rolling slowly can have more energy than a marble rolling fast. Bowling pins fly because the ball is both heavy and quick. When you look at a moving object, ask two questions. How fast is it going? How much mass does it have? Together they tell you how much energy it carries.

words.d: the ability to make something happen, such as moving, warming or lighting an object
the energy an object has because it is moving; more speed or more mass means more of it

look.title: Everyday Speeds
look.prompt: If all of these had the same mass, which would carry the most motion energy? Why does a car crash usually do more damage than a bike crash?

check.q: What does energy let an object do?
choices: Make something happen, such as move or warm another object
check.why: Energy is the ability to make things happen. You see it through its effects.

check.q: Two identical balls roll toward you. One is faster. Which is true?
choices: The slower ball has more energy
The faster ball has more energy
Neither has energy until it hits you
check.why: With the same mass, the faster object carries more motion energy.

check.q: A bowling ball and a marble roll at the same speed. Why does the bowling ball knock more pins down?
choices: It has more mass, so more energy
check.why: At the same speed, the object with more mass carries more motion energy.

lessons.title: Energy Passes in a Collision
lessons.mainIdea: When objects collide, energy moves from one object to the other, and the motion of both changes.
reading: The marble hits the first domino. The marble slows. The domino starts to fall. Energy has moved from the marble to the domino. This is a *collision*, when two objects hit each other. In every collision, some energy passes from one object to another. The one that was moving loses some. The one that was hit gains some.

Watch a game of pool. The white ball rolls and smacks a striped ball. The white ball stops or slows. The striped ball zips off. Nearly all the motion energy jumped from one ball to the other. The energy did not vanish. It just changed owners. Scientists say energy is *transferred*, which means moved from one thing to another.

Not all the energy goes into motion. Listen to the click when the balls hit. That sound is energy too. Touch the balls after a long game and they feel slightly warm. Some energy became heat. When you add up the motion, the sound, and the heat, the total stays the same. Energy is never created or destroyed. It only changes form or moves along.

words.d: when two objects hit each other
moved from one object or place to another

look.title: Five Steel Balls
look.text: Five steel balls hang in a row from strings, each just touching the next. Pull the ball on one end back and let it drop. It hits the row. The three middle balls do not seem to move. But the ball on the far end swings out, almost as high as the first ball was dropped. Then it swings back, and the first ball flies out again. Click, click, click.
look.prompt: How did energy get from the first ball to the last one when the middle balls barely moved? Why does each swing get a little smaller?

check.q: A rolling marble hits a still marble and stops. The second marble rolls away. What happened to the energy?
choices: It was transferred to the second marble
It stayed in the first marble
check.why: In a collision, energy moves from the moving object to the one it hits.

check.q: What is a collision?
choices: An object rolling down a ramp
check.why: A collision is when two objects hit. Energy passes between them when they do.

check.q: After many collisions, pool balls feel slightly warm. Where did that heat come from?
choices: From the lights above the table
From some of the motion energy changing into heat
From the felt on the table
check.why: Each collision turns a little motion energy into heat and sound. The total energy stays the same.

lessons.title: Stored Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Food, fuel, batteries and a marble held up high all store energy that can be released later.
reading: The marble at the top of the tower is still, yet it can make the bell ring. It holds *stored energy* because it is high up. The higher it starts, the more it stores. Let it go and gravity turns the stored energy into motion. A stretched rubber band stores energy the same way. Let it go and the energy snaps out.

Food stores energy too. Your body takes energy from bread, rice, and beans. That energy moves your muscles and keeps you warm. A car's engine takes energy from *fuel* like gasoline. Gasoline burns, and the energy pushes the car. The energy in food and fuel is locked inside the tiny bits they are made of. Burning or digesting sets it loose.

A *battery* stores energy in chemicals sealed inside a case. Connect it to a wire and the chemicals slowly change, pushing electricity out. When the chemicals are used up, the battery is dead. Stored energy is useful because you decide when to use it. A marble on a shelf, a sandwich, a tank of gas, and a battery are all waiting for you.

words.d: energy an object holds and can release later, such as a raised marble or a charged battery
a material, such as gasoline or wood, that releases stored energy when it burns
a sealed case of chemicals that stores energy and pushes out electricity

look.title: Energy Stored in Food
look.prompt: One gram of fat and one gram of sugar: which stores more energy? Why might a hiker pack nuts instead of candy?

check.q: Which marble has the most stored energy from height?
choices: A marble on a low step
A marble on top of a tall shelf
check.why: The higher an object is, the more energy it stores to release when it falls.

check.q: Where does the energy in a battery come from?
check.why: A battery stores energy in its chemicals. As they change, they push electricity out.

check.q: Why is a stretched rubber band an example of stored energy?
choices: It can release energy and move when let go
check.why: The stretched band holds energy. When you let go, that energy becomes motion.

lessons.title: Sound Carries Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Sound is energy that travels through air, water and solids as vibrations.
reading: The bell in the marble run rings. Across the room, you hear it. Energy traveled from the bell to your ear with nothing carrying it that you could see. The bell starts to *vibrate*, shaking back and forth very fast. The shaking bumps the air next to it. That air bumps the next bit of air. The bumps spread out like ripples on a pond. This traveling shake is *sound*.

Sound needs something to travel through. Air works. Water works even better. Solids work best of all. Put your ear on a table and tap the far end. The tap sounds loud and sharp. Sound carries real energy. A loud speaker can make a glass of water ripple. A big drum thumps in your chest. Very loud sounds can even shatter a glass.

Sound is fast, but not instant. Watch a batter hit a ball from far away. You see the swing, then hear the crack a moment later. In air, sound travels about 343 meters each second. That is about the length of three football fields. Light gets to your eye almost at once. So the sight arrives first and the sound trails behind.

words.d: to shake back and forth very quickly
energy that travels as vibrations through air, water or solids

look.title: How Fast Sound Travels
look.prompt: Sound travels much faster in steel than in air. Why might a person hear a far-off train sooner by listening at the rail than by listening in the air?

check.q: What is a vibrating object doing?
check.why: To vibrate means to shake back and forth fast. That shaking makes sound.

check.q: You see a far-off batter swing, then hear the crack a moment later. Why?
choices: The batter hit the ball twice
The sound was stored in the bat
Your eyes are slower than your ears
Sound travels much slower than light
check.why: Light reaches you almost instantly. Sound moves at about 343 m/s, so it arrives later.

check.q: Which shows that sound carries energy?
choices: A loud speaker makes water in a glass ripple
A ball rolls down a hill
check.why: The sound made the water move. Making something happen takes energy.

lessons.title: Light Carries Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Light carries energy from a source across space, even through empty space, and can warm what it lands on.
reading: Stand in a sunny window. Your skin feels warm. That warmth came from the Sun, about 150 million kilometers away. It rode here on *light*. Light is energy that travels from a *source*, such as the Sun, a flame, or a bulb. Unlike sound, light does not need air. It crosses empty space with ease. That is how sunlight reaches Earth.

When light lands on something, it gives up energy. A dark car seat gets hot in the sun. Plants catch light and use its energy to make food. A solar panel turns light into electricity. Some light bounces off instead. That bouncing light is what lets you see. Your eye catches light that came from a source and bounced off the world.

Light is the fastest thing we know. It travels about 300,000 kilometers every second. Sunlight takes a bit over 8 minutes to reach Earth. When you look at the Sun's light, you are seeing energy that left the Sun 8 minutes ago. Light from distant stars left them long before you were born. The site's telescope collects that light and lets you see it.

words.d: energy that travels from a source, such as the Sun or a bulb, and can cross empty space
where something comes from; a light source gives off light

look.title: Two Cups in the Sun
look.text: Fill two paper cups with cold water. Wrap one in black paper and one in white paper. Set both in a sunny spot for an hour. Then feel the water in each cup. Now imagine doing the same test at night under a bright lamp, and again inside a closet with the door shut.
look.prompt: Which cup will be warmer in the sun, and why? What would you expect in the closet?

check.q: How does the Sun's energy reach Earth?
choices: Carried by light across empty space
It does not; Earth makes its own heat
check.why: Light does not need air. It carries energy across the empty space between the Sun and Earth.

check.q: A black car seat gets hot in the sun. What happened?
choices: The seat made its own energy
Light gave its energy to the seat
check.why: When light lands on an object, it gives up energy, which warms the object.

check.q: Why can you see a ball on the floor?
choices: The ball gives off its own light
Light from a source bounces off the ball into your eye
check.why: You see most things by light that bounced off them and reached your eye.

lessons.title: Heat Moves From Hot to Cold
lessons.mainIdea: Heat is energy that always moves from a warmer object to a cooler one.
reading: Hold a mug of hot cocoa. Your hands warm up. The cocoa cools down. Energy moved from the hot drink to your cooler hands. This moving energy is *heat*. Heat always travels from warmer to cooler, never the other way on its own. A cold spoon in hot soup warms up. A hot spoon in cold water cools down. The energy flows until both are the same temperature.

Heat moves in a few ways. It passes through solids, which is why a metal spoon in soup gets hot at the handle. It rides on moving air and water, which is how a radiator warms a whole room. And it travels as light, which is how a campfire warms your face from a distance. Metals pass heat quickly. Wood, plastic, and air pass it slowly.

A material that slows heat down is called an *insulator*. A winter coat traps air to keep your body's heat in. A foam cup keeps cocoa hot. An ice chest keeps the cold in and the summer heat out. In Chicago, homes stuff insulation in walls and attics. Less heat leaks out in January, so the furnace burns less fuel.

words.d: energy that moves from a warmer object to a cooler one
a material that slows the movement of heat, such as foam, wool or trapped air

look.title: Heat From a Cannon Shop
look.text: In 1798, Benjamin Thompson, known as Count Rumford, watched brass cannons being bored in a workshop in Munich. The metal grew hot enough to boil water, and it kept giving off heat as long as the boring went on. He reported that the supply of heat seemed to have no end. Anything a body could keep giving out without limit, he argued, could not be a material substance. He concluded that heat was a kind of motion.
look.cite: Count Rumford, paper read to the Royal Society, 1798 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What did Rumford observe, and why did it make him doubt that heat was a kind of fluid stored inside the metal?

check.q: A cold spoon is put in hot soup. Which way does heat move?
choices: From the soup to the spoon
From the spoon to the soup
check.why: Heat moves from the warmer object to the cooler one, so it flows from soup to spoon.

check.q: Why does a foam cup keep cocoa hot longer than a metal cup?
choices: Foam is an insulator that slows heat leaving
check.why: Foam traps air and passes heat slowly. Metal passes heat quickly.

check.q: What did Rumford notice about cannon boring?
choices: The rubbing kept making heat as long as it continued
check.why: The heat never ran out while the boring went on, which made him think heat was motion.

lessons.title: Wires Carry Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Electricity moves energy through wires from where it is made to where it is used.
reading: Flip a switch and a lamp across the room glows. The energy for that light did not start in the lamp. It came through a wire. *Electricity* is energy moving through wires as a flow of tiny charges. It is a fast and handy way to move energy from place to place. Power plants far outside Chicago send energy along wires to homes across the city.

Electricity needs a complete path, called a *circuit*. Think of it as a loop. Energy leaves a battery, travels along a wire, passes through a bulb, and returns along another wire. If the loop has a gap, the flow stops and the bulb goes dark. A *switch* is just a gap you can open and close. Open the gap, off. Close it, on.

Try it with a battery, two wires, and a small bulb. Touch one wire to each end of the battery and the other ends to the bulb. The bulb lights. Pull one wire off and it goes dark. Now put a paper clip in the loop; it still lights. Put a plastic straw in the loop, and nothing. Metals let electricity through. Plastic and rubber block it.

words.d: energy carried by a flow of tiny charges through a wire
a complete loop that electricity can flow around
a gap in a circuit that you can open to stop the flow or close to let it through

look.title: Volta's Pile
look.text: In a letter written in 1800, Alessandro Volta described stacking pairs of silver and zinc disks with a piece of wet cardboard or cloth between each pair. Touching the top and bottom of the pile with wet fingers gave a shock, and the pile kept working for as long as he wanted. A rubbed glass, by contrast, had to be rubbed again after each spark. This pile was the first battery.
look.cite: Alessandro Volta, letter to the Royal Society of London, 1800 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: How was Volta's pile different from the static charge on a rubbed balloon?

check.q: What happens when a circuit has a gap in it?
choices: The energy flows through the air
The flow stops and the bulb goes dark
check.why: Electricity needs a complete loop. A gap breaks the loop and stops the flow.

check.q: Which object would let a circuit keep working if placed in the loop?
check.why: Metals let electricity through. Plastic, rubber, and wood block it.

check.q: What does a switch do in a circuit?
choices: Opens or closes a gap in the loop
check.why: A switch is a gap you control. Closing it lets electricity flow; opening it stops the flow.

lessons.title: From Battery to Light and Motion
lessons.mainIdea: A circuit changes the stored energy in a battery into light, motion, sound or heat.
reading: A flashlight is a tiny energy machine. Chemicals in the battery hold stored energy. Close the switch and the circuit carries that energy to the bulb. The bulb turns it into light and a little heat. Touch a flashlight bulb that has been on a while. It is warm. The energy took three forms: stored, then electric, then light and heat.

Swap the bulb for a small *motor* and the same energy becomes motion. A motor uses electricity and magnets to spin a shaft. Add a fan blade and you have a breeze. Add wheels and you have a toy car. Swap in a *buzzer* and the energy becomes sound. Every device in the circuit changes electric energy into a form you want.

Think about your day. An alarm clock changes electricity into sound. A toaster changes it into heat. A phone screen changes it into light. An electric train on Chicago's rails changes it into motion. Each device is a converter. Follow any device back and you find a battery or a plug. Follow the plug back and you reach a power plant.

words.d: a device that uses electricity and magnets to make something spin
a device that changes electricity into sound

look.title: The Flashlight Test
look.text: A student has a flashlight, a fresh battery, and an old battery that has been used for a year. With the fresh battery, the bulb is bright white. With the old battery, the bulb glows a dim orange. She leaves the flashlight on with the fresh battery. After a few hours the light is dimmer. After a whole night, it is dark.
look.prompt: Where did the fresh battery's energy go? What evidence shows that a battery stores a limited amount?

check.q: In a flashlight, what changes electricity into light?
check.why: The battery stores energy and the wires carry it, but the bulb is the part that makes light.

check.q: What does a motor do in a circuit?
check.why: A motor uses electricity and magnets to spin, turning electric energy into motion.

check.q: A flashlight bulb feels warm after being on. What does that tell you?
choices: Some of the energy became heat, not just light
The bulb is making extra energy
Light and heat are the same thing
check.why: The bulb changes some energy into light and some into heat. No energy is made or lost.

lessons.title: Designing an Energy Changer
lessons.mainIdea: Engineers design devices that change energy from one form to another, then test and improve them.
reading: Here is a challenge. Build a device that uses a marble's stored energy to ring a bell. You have tubes, tape, dominoes, a bell, and a marble. That is exactly what the cousins built. It is also what engineers do all day. They *design* devices that change energy from one form into a form people need. A wind turbine changes moving air into electricity. A solar oven changes light into heat.

Good design starts with a clear goal. What must the device do? Then comes a *prototype*, a first rough version. The cousins' first prototype flung the marble off the table. That failure gave them information. They added a curved tube. Test, look at what happened, change one thing, test again. Each round makes the design better.

Try one yourself. Line a shoebox with foil. Paint the bottom black or cover it with black paper. Cover the top with clear plastic wrap. Set it in the sun with a chocolate chip inside. This is a solar oven. It changes light into heat. Does the chip melt? How long does it take? What one change would make it hotter? That question is where engineering begins.

words.d: to plan and build something to solve a problem or meet a goal
a first rough version of a device, built to be tested

look.title: Wind at the Lakefront
look.text: Along Lake Michigan the wind almost never stops. A class wants to build a device that uses that moving air to lift a small weight on a string. They have paper, straws, a pencil, tape, a spool, and string. One team builds a pinwheel. Another builds a sail on a cart. A third builds paper cups on a stick that spins.
look.prompt: Which design would you test first for lifting the weight, and what would you measure to decide which team's device works best?

check.q: What is a prototype?
choices: A first rough version built for testing
A drawing that is never built
check.why: A prototype is an early version. Testing it shows what to change.

check.q: The cousins' marble flew off the table. What was the best next step?
choices: Change one thing and test again
check.why: A failed test is information. Change one thing, such as adding a curved tube, and test again.

check.q: Which device changes light energy into heat?
check.why: A solar oven catches sunlight and turns its energy into heat inside the box.

lessons.title: Testing and Improving
lessons.mainIdea: A fair test, where only one thing changes at a time, shows which design change actually helps.
reading: You built a solar oven and the chip melted in 20 minutes. Now you want it faster. You could change the foil, the box size, the color, and the plastic all at once. But if it works better, which change did it? You would not know. A *fair test* changes only one thing at a time. Keep everything else the same. Then the result has one clear cause.

Make a *data table*. Write down what you changed and what you measured. Trial 1: white paper inside, 20 minutes. Trial 2: black paper inside, 12 minutes. Trial 3: black paper and a second layer of plastic, 9 minutes. Now the numbers tell a story. Black paper helped. The second layer helped more. Evidence, not guessing, guides the next step.

Engineers also weigh trade-offs. A bigger oven catches more light but is harder to carry. A thicker box holds heat but costs more. There is rarely one perfect design. There is the design that best fits the goal. Share your data with another team. Compare results. Science and engineering are team sports. The best ideas come from many tests and many minds.

words.d: a test that changes only one thing at a time so you know what caused the result
a chart where you record what you changed and what you measured

look.title: Reading the Oven Table
look.text: A team's data table shows four solar oven trials on the same sunny afternoon. White paper inside, one plastic layer: 20 minutes to melt the chip. Black paper, one layer: 12 minutes. Black paper, two layers: 9 minutes. Black paper, two layers, and a foil flap to bounce in extra sunlight: 7 minutes. Each trial changed only one thing from the trial before.
look.prompt: Which single change helped the most? What would you test next, and what would you keep the same?

check.q: What makes a test fair?
choices: Changing only one thing at a time
check.why: If only one thing changes, you know that change caused the result.

check.q: Trial 1 used white paper and took 20 minutes. Trial 2 used black paper and took 12. What can you conclude?
choices: Black paper helped the oven heat faster
check.why: Only the paper color changed between the trials, so the paper caused the faster melt.

check.q: What is a trade-off in design?
choices: Giving up one good thing to get another
check.why: A bigger oven catches more light but is harder to carry. Choosing between them is a trade-off.

review.q: Why does a taller marble run make the marble hit harder at the bottom?
choices: The marble stores more energy when it starts higher
Gravity gets stronger at the top
review.why: Height stores energy. More height means more stored energy that becomes motion on the way down.

review.q: Which object has the most motion energy?
review.why: The truck has the most mass and the highest speed, so it carries the most motion energy.

review.q: Which is the best example of energy being transferred by a collision?
choices: A plant growing in the sun
A cue ball hitting another ball and stopping
A battery sitting in a drawer
review.why: The cue ball's motion energy passed to the other ball when they hit.

review.q: Which of these needs no air to travel?
review.why: Light crosses empty space. Sound and ripples need something to travel through.

review.q: A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot at the handle. Which way did heat move?
choices: From the hot soup to the cooler handle
From the handle to the soup
From the air to the soup
review.why: Heat moves from warmer to cooler, passing along the metal to the handle.

review.q: A bulb in a circuit will not light. What is the most likely reason?
choices: There is a gap somewhere in the loop
The battery has too much energy
review.why: Electricity needs a complete loop. A gap anywhere stops the flow.

review.q: Which change of energy happens in a toaster?
review.why: A toaster is a converter that changes electric energy into heat.

review.q: A team's first solar oven design fails. What should they do next?
choices: Throw it away and start over
Change one thing, test again, and record the result
review.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time so the team learns what helped.
